chapters.title: Chapter 3: Behavioral Economics in Pricing, Business, and Negotiation

lessons.title: Herd Behavior at Market Scale: Bubbles, Bank Runs, and Systemic Panic

children.text: Back in Chapter 1, you saw depositors queue outside a financially healthy cooperative bank simply because news of a different, troubled bank was fresh in their minds, the availability heuristic doing exactly what it does. That explains why the first few depositors panicked. It does not explain why the queue kept growing even among people who never saw the news at all, and who privately doubted anything was wrong. This closing lesson of Chapter 3 explains that second, more unsettling layer: how perfectly rational individuals, copying other rational individuals, can turn a healthy institution into a failed one without a single person along the way making an obvious mistake.

body.text: Market-scale herding isn't always many people being individually biased at the same time. Often it is individually rational people correctly responding to what everyone else is doing, in a situation where everyone else doing the same thing changes the outcome. That distinction is the difference between a bias you can educate away and a trap that catches rational people on purpose.

children.text: Information Cascades: When Copying Others Is Individually Rational

markDefs.definition: A situation where people rationally ignore their own private information and instead copy the observed actions of others, because the accumulated pattern of others' choices appears to carry more information than any one person's own signal.

children.text: In 1992, economist Abhijit Banerjee, and separately Sushil Bikhchandani, David Hirshleifer, and Ivo Welch, formalized what is now called an

. Economists illustrate it with two identical new restaurants opening side by side. Each diner has a weak private hunch about which is better, correct only slightly more often than a coin flip, and can also see which restaurant earlier diners chose. Once one restaurant is even slightly fuller than the other, later diners rationally reason that the accumulated choices of everyone before them carry more information than their own single weak hunch, and pile into the fuller restaurant, even overriding their own private signal to the contrary. Every individual decision along the way is perfectly rational. The restaurant that ends up empty may well have been the better one.
Strategic Complementarity: When Your Best Move Depends on What Everyone Else Does

markDefs.definition: A situation where taking a particular action becomes more rewarding, or safer, the more other people also take it, which is what allows shared belief alone to determine the outcome, independent of the underlying fundamentals.

children.text: Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig modeled the sharper version of this in a landmark 1983 paper on bank runs, work that earned them, alongside Ben Bernanke, the 2022 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. A bank takes short-term deposits and lends them out long-term, a mismatch that works perfectly well as long as only a normal fraction of depositors ask for their money on any given day. This creates

: if you believe enough other depositors are about to withdraw, your own rational best move is to withdraw too, immediately, regardless of whether you actually believe the bank is insolvent, because a bank cannot liquidate long-term loans fast enough to pay everyone at once. The same bank, with the exact same underlying loans and the exact same fundamentals, survives if everyone believes everyone else will stay calm, and fails if everyone believes everyone else will run. Nothing about the bank's actual health has to change for the outcome to flip.

body.text: This is what makes a bank run different from an ordinary bias. Reassuring an individual depositor that the bank is fine doesn't fix the problem, because their decision was never really about whether the bank is fine. It was about what they expect everyone else to do. You cannot argue someone out of a correct prediction about a stampede.

children.text: Deposit Insurance: A Policy Tool Aimed at Killing the Cascade

In September 2019, the RBI placed restrictions on Punjab and Maharashtra Co-operative Bank after uncovering serious financial irregularities, a real, well-documented event, and the same kind of shock that drove the generic cooperative-bank scenario in Chapter 1. The policy response arrived a few months later: in the Union Budget of February 2020, the government raised the DICGC deposit insurance cover from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh per depositor, per bank. This is worth naming precisely because, unlike the nudges covered throughout this course, deposit insurance is not a nudge at all. It directly changes the economic payoff of panicking. If your deposit is guaranteed regardless of whether you are first in line or last, strategic complementarity collapses: your best move no longer depends on what anyone else does, because you get your money back either way, up to the insured limit. It is a solution built for the actual game-theoretic structure of the problem, not merely for the psychology of the depositor.

children.text: IPO Herding: Cascades in Real Time

Indian IPOs display information cascades almost in slow motion. Subscription numbers and unofficial grey market premium figures are published while the issue is still open, giving later applicants exactly the kind of visible, accumulating public signal the restaurant example describes. A retail investor with no strong independent view on the company's fundamentals can watch an issue go from undersubscribed to oversubscribed within hours and rationally treat that shift as new information worth acting on, even though the underlying business hasn't changed at all in that time. Chapter 6 returns to this same mechanism at full scale, tracing how it builds into asset bubbles and business cycles well beyond a single IPO window.

body.title: Two IPOs, one signal
body.scenario: Rahul is deciding between applying for two IPOs closing the same day. He has read both companies' filings and has a mild, low-confidence preference for Company A. Two hours before close, he checks the subscription data: Company A is subscribed 1.2 times, Company B is subscribed 40 times.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's framework, is it necessarily irrational for Rahul to switch his application to Company B?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Not necessarily. If Rahul genuinely believes the subscription gap partly reflects other applicants' private research and information he doesn't have access to, following the crowd's revealed signal over his own weak, low-confidence preference can be a rational information cascade, exactly like the restaurant example.
2. It becomes less rational the more Rahul suspects the 40x figure itself is partly self-reinforcing, driven by earlier applicants who were themselves just reacting to the subscription number rather than to independent research, a cascade feeding on itself rather than on real information.
3. A useful check is to ask what specifically he believes the other 40x worth of applicants know that he doesn't, rather than simply reacting to the number itself. If he can't identify any real informational advantage they plausibly have, he is likely witnessing a cascade rather than genuine collective wisdom.
4. Either way, this decision should be treated as separate from his own fundamentals-based analysis of Company A, not as evidence that his own research was wrong. The cascade explains the crowd's behavior. It does not automatically make the crowd correct.

body.title: Bias, or rational cascade?
body.question: Which of these is the clearest example of strategic complementarity rather than a simple cognitive bias?
options: An investor overestimates crash risk right after a vividly reported market crash story
A depositor withdraws funds from a fundamentally healthy bank specifically because they believe enough other depositors are about to withdraw first
A shopper assumes a well-known brand's new product must be safe because the brand itself is trusted
A hiring manager assumes a candidate is a strong fit because their resume resembles a stereotype of a good employee
body.explanation: Option B is strategic complementarity: the depositor's own best move genuinely depends on what they expect others to do, not on a misfiring mental shortcut. The other three are, respectively, the availability heuristic, the affect heuristic, and the representativeness heuristic, all from Chapter 1, each a cognitive shortcut rather than a rational response to others' expected actions.

body.title: Name the mechanism
body.textWithBlank: A situation where taking an action becomes more rewarding the more other people also take it, which allows shared belief alone to determine an outcome, is called strategic ___.
body.explanation: Strategic complementarity is why bank runs, currency attacks, and certain market stampedes can happen to a fundamentally sound institution, purely because enough people believe enough other people will act first.

body.title: Can the exact same bank really have two different fates?

children.text: Yes, and this is precisely what economists mean by multiple equilibria. The Diamond-Dybvig model shows that, for a normal bank taking short-term deposits and making long-term loans, both "everyone stays calm, the bank survives" and "everyone panics, the bank fails" can be mathematically stable outcomes for the exact same underlying balance sheet. Which one actually happens depends on which belief people coordinate around, not on any change in the bank's fundamentals. This is a large part of why deposit insurance, and in more extreme cases a central bank acting as lender of last resort, exist: not to fix a bank's finances, but to make the panic equilibrium impossible to reach in the first place, a theme Chapter 6 develops fully when it covers central bank policy.

body.label: India's deposit insurance cover today
body.context: Raised from ₹1 lakh in the February 2020 Union Budget, following the September 2019 restrictions on Punjab and Maharashtra Co-operative Bank.

A guarantee, run in India by the DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, that directly removes the incentive to panic-withdraw by changing the actual economic payoff, not merely the psychology, of waiting.
A central bank's role in supplying emergency liquidity to solvent banks facing a run, to prevent a panic equilibrium from being reached, covered fully in Chapter 6.

points: Market-scale herding has two distinct roots: individually irrational biases like the availability heuristic, and individually rational responses to what others are doing, information cascades and strategic complementarity, which is the far more dangerous kind because education alone can't fix it.

An information cascade happens when people rationally treat others' visible choices as more informative than their own weak private signal, which is why a crowd's behavior is not automatically evidence the crowd is right.

Strategic complementarity, formalized in Diamond and Dybvig's Nobel Prize-winning 1983 model, explains how a fundamentally healthy bank can fail purely because enough depositors expect enough other depositors to withdraw first.

India's deposit insurance, raised to ₹5 lakh per depositor after the 2019 PMC Bank episode, works by changing the actual payoff of panicking, not by persuading anyone the bank is safe, which is exactly why it succeeds where reassurance alone would not.

This closes the throughline of Chapter 3: anchoring, decoys, and loss framing shape individual decisions, and information cascades and strategic complementarity are what happen when enough of those individual decisions start reacting to each other. Chapter 4 turns to how Indian public policy deliberately designs around exactly this.
